chapters.title: Section 1
chapters.content:
11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

@ BetterHealth

Vitamins and minerals

Summary

e Eating plenty of fruits, vegetables, wholegrains and cereals, lean meats and reduced fat
dairy products will give your body the vitamins and minerals it needs, at the right level
and in the right balance.

e There are 13 vitamins in total - 8 of these come from the B-group of vitamins.

chapters.title: Section 2
chapters.content:
¢ Vitamins and minerals are essential for bodily functions such as helping to fight infection,
wound healing, making our bones strong and regulating hormones.

e Vitamins and minerals can cause toxicity if consumed in large amounts.

About vitamins and minerals

Vitamins and minerals are organic compounds that our bodies use in very small

amounts for a variety of metabolic processes. Basically, they keep us healthy and

help our bodies to function.

chapters.title: Section 3
chapters.content:
We get vitamins and minerals from the foods we eat. For most of us, a healthy and

varied diet

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/healthy-eating)

(that includes all 5 food groups) is all we need to stay healthy. It is best to get

vitamins and minerals from eating a variety of healthy unrefined foods.

Vitamins and minerals can cause toxicity if consumed in large amounts.

Types of vitamins and their functions

chapters.title: Section 4
chapters.content:
Vitamins and minerals are a form of nutrient (called micronutrients) that are needed

in small amounts. Although micronutrients don’t give us energy

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/energy-in-and-energy-out)

, they are involved in the metabolic processes that enable us to get energy from

https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 117

chapters.title: Section 5
chapters.content:
11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel
carbohydrates
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/carbohydrates-and-the-glycaemic-
index)

, protein

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/protein)

and fat

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/fats-and-oils)

, which are also known as macronutrients.

Different vitamins serve different purposes and contribute to different bodily

chapters.title: Section 6
chapters.content:
functions. There are 13 vitamins in total and 8 of these come from the B-group of

vitamins.

Vitamin A

Vitamin A is important because it:

« makes the immune system
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/immune-system)
work effectively so it can fight disease and infections
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/infections-bacterial-and-viral)

e keeps our skin
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/skin)
healthy

chapters.title: Section 7
chapters.content:
¢ supports reproduction and growth

e helps with vision
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/eyes)

Food sources of vitamin A

There are different compounds with vitamin A activity in animal and plant foods.

Plant foods can be easy to spot as they tend to have orange/yellow pigment known

as beta-carotene.

Plant sources include:

¢ orange and yellow fruit and vegetables
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/fruit-and-vegetables)

chapters.title: Section 8
chapters.content:
- such as carrots, red capsicum, mangoes, sweet potatoes, apricots, pumpkin and
cantaloupe

e leafy green vegetables - such as spinach, peas and broccoli.

https://(www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 217

chapters.title: Section 9
chapters.content:
11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel
Animal sources include:
e liver
* eggs
¢ some fortified milk
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/milk)
and milk products (with added vitamin A).
Vitamin A deficiency risks
Because of the various roles that vitamin A plays in the body, deficiency can have
several health effects. These include:
e increased risk of infections
e night blindness and irreversible blindness (xeropthalmia)
e« excessive keratin build-up of the skin.
Vitamin B
B-group vitamins
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/vitamin-b)
help our bodies use the energy-yielding nutrients (such as carbohydrates, fat and
protein) for fuel. Some B-group vitamins are needed to help cells to multiply by
making new DNA.
Except for B-12 and folate which are stored by the liver, most B-group vitamins can't
be stored by the body. They must be consumed regularly in a healthy diet that
includes a range of wholefoods (such as lean meat
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Meat-and-poultry)
_ fish
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/fish)
, wholegrains
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/cereals-and-wholegrain-foods)
, fruit, vegetables and legumes) and limits the intake of alcohol
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/alcohol)
and processed foods.
The 8 types of vitamin B are:
e thiamin (B1)
¢ riboflavin (B2)
https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 3/17

chapters.title: Section 10
chapters.content:
11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

e niacin (B3)

e pantothenic acid (B5)

¢ pyridoxine (B6)

e biotin (B7)

e folate or ‘folic acid’ when included in supplements (B9)

e¢ cyanocobalamin (B12).

A person who has a poor diet for a few months may end up with B-group vitamins

deficiency. For this reason, it’s important that adequate amounts of these vitamins

be eaten regularly as part of a well-balanced, nutritious diet.

Vitamin C

chapters.title: Section 11
chapters.content:
Dietary intake of vitamin C (from food and drinks) is essential, because the human

body cannot make this vitamin from other compounds. We also need to have

vitamin C as a regular part of our diet because the body cannot store vitamin C for

very long.

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is important for many metabolic processes, including:

chapters.title: Section 12
chapters.content:
¢ Collagen formation - collagen is used in different ways throughout the body. Its primary
role is to strengthen the skin, blood vessels and bone. The body also relies on collagen to
heal wounds.

chapters.title: Section 13
chapters.content:
e Antioxidant function
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/antioxidants)
- the metabolism of oxygen within the body releases molecular compounds called ‘free
radicals’, which damage cell membranes. Antioxidants are substances that destroy free
radicals, and vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant.

chapters.title: Section 14
chapters.content:
e lron absorption
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/iron)
- the process of iron absorption is aided by vitamin C, particularly non-haem iron (found in
plant foods such as beans and lentils).

¢ Infection fighting - the immune system
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/immune-system)
, particularly cells called lymphocytes, requires vitamin C for proper functioning.

chapters.title: Section 15
chapters.content:
e Other roles - vitamin C is used to produce other important substances in the body such as
brain chemicals (neurotransmitters).

https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 417

11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

Dietary sources of vitamin C

Adults need about 45mg of vitamin C per day and any excess amount (above

200mg) is excreted.

Vitamin C is sensitive to heat, so some of its nutritional benefits can be lost during

chapters.title: Section 16
chapters.content:
cooking. Raw foods are more beneficial as dietary sources of vitamin C. These

include:

e fruit - oranges, lemons, limes, grapefruits, blackcurrants, mangoes, kiwifruits, rock melon,
tomatoes and strawberries

¢ vegetables - particularly green vegetables (such as cabbage, capsicum, spinach, Brussels
sprouts, lettuce and broccoli), cauliflower and potatoes.

Vitamin C deficiency and scurvy

A severe lack of vitamin C can lead to scurvy. We may think of it as a disease of the

chapters.title: Section 17
chapters.content:
past, but it does still exist. Factors or lifestyle issues that may increase your scurvy

risk include:

e regularly eating unhealthy foods

e crash dieting
(bttp://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/weight-loss-q-healthy-approach)
- especially being on diets that exclude certain food groups

¢ being malnourished due to inadequate care

¢ very strict allergy diets
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/food-allergy-and-intolerance)

chapters.title: Section 18
chapters.content:
¢ having an eating disorder
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/eating-disorders)

e smoking
(http://www. betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/smoking-tobacco-is-deadly)
- smokers need more vitamin C to cope with the extra stress on their body.

Scurvy symptoms

The onset of symptoms of scurvy depends on how long it takes for the person to use

up their limited stores of vitamin C.

Scurvy is usually easy to treat - symptoms are like many other mild complaints and

may include:

¢ fatigue
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/fatigue)
and generally feeling unwell
e loss of appetite
* nausea and diarrhoea
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/diarrhoea)
e fever
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/fever)
e painful joints and muscles
e¢ small ‘pinpoint’ bleeding around hair follicles visible in the skin.
If you or someone you care for is at risk, please see your doctor.
Vitamin D
Vitamin D
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/vitamin-d)
is important for strong bones, muscles and overall health. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation
from the sun is necessary to produce vitamin D in the skin and is the best natural
source of vitamin D.
Regular physical activity
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov. Ith, Ithyliving/sports-and-physical-activity)
also assists with the body’s production of vitamin D.
The body can only absorb small amounts of Vitamin D.
Spending too much time in the sun may increase your risk of skin cancer
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/skin-cancer)
. Remember to use daily sun protection
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/skin-cancer-risk-factors)
, especially at times when UV index levels are at their highest (3 or above).
Food sources of vitamin D
Only a small amount (around 5-10%) of Vitamin D is sourced from our diet. Sources
include:
¢ fatty fish
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/fish)
(such as salmon)
https://(www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 6/17

chapters.title: Section 21
chapters.content:
11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel
° eggs
* margarine and some milks have added vitamin D.
Vitamin D deficiency
It is important to achieve a good peak bone mass early in life. Vitamin D deficiency
can result in a decline in bone density in adult life, increasing the risk of:
e osteoporosis
(http://www. betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/osteoporosis)
¢ falls
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/falls-prevention-at-home)
and bone fractures
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/bone-fractures)
(especially for older people)
¢ rickets
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/rickets)
(in young children) - a preventable bone disease
Treatment options include improved sunlight exposure, diet, exercise, vitamin and
mineral supplements
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/vitamin-and-minerals)
If you are concerned about vitamin D levels, see your GP. Your GP may recommend
vitamin D supplements, which should be taken strictly as directed.
Vitamin E
Vitamin E is an antioxidant
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/antioxidants)
that helps protect your body against damage from free radicals, such as exposure
to cigarette smoke or radiation. It is also important for our:
* vision
e« immune system
e skin.
Dietary sources of vitamin E
Vitamin E is best obtained from a healthy diet that contains plenty of fresh
minimally processed foods
https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals TAT

chapters.content:
11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/food-processing-and-nutrition)

. Vitamin E is also vulnerable to heat (especially cooking methods such as deep

frying.

Dietary sources include:

¢ meats (eg. liver)
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Meat-and-poultry)

* egg yolks

e leafy green vegetables - spinach, broccoli

chapters.title: Section 23
chapters.content:
* nuts and seeds
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Nuts-and-seeds)
- such as almonds, sunflower seeds, peanuts and hazelnuts

e healthy oils
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/fats-and-oils)
- such as extra virgin, sunflower, soybean

¢ unprocessed cereals and wholegrains
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/cereals-and-wholegrain-foods)
- such as wheat germ.

Vitamin E deficiency

chapters.title: Section 24
chapters.content:
Deficiency is rare but can happen in people with diseases that cause fat

malabsorption (like cystic fibrosis

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/cystic-fibrosis-cf)

Erythrocyte haemolysis is another deficiency - it’s seen in infants born before

vitamin E is transferred to them from their mother prior to birth.

Vitamin K

Vitamin K is important for:

e healthy bones

e¢ blood clotting and wound healing

chapters.title: Section 25
chapters.content:
e newborn babies
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/vitamin-k-and-newborn-babies)
to prevent a serious bleeding condition called haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (HDN).

https://www.betterhealth. vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 8/17

11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

Dietary sources of vitamin K

chapters.title: Section 26
chapters.content:
We get vitamin K from food and the bacteria in our gastrointestinal tract. Newborn
babies are given a booster to increase their vitamin K levels because they are born
without bacteria in their gastrointestinal tract. We get much of our vitamin K from
our diet.

Food sources include:

e leafy green vegetables - spinach and kale

e fruits - such as avocado and kiwi fruit

« some vegetable oils - such as soybean oil.

Vitamin K deficiency

chapters.title: Section 27
chapters.content:
Vitamin K deficiency is unlikely except when fat is not absorbed properly or when
certain medications are used. For example, antibiotics can kill the gastrointestinal
bacteria that produce vitamin K.

Additionally, anticoagulant drugs (or blood thinners) may cause problems with
vitamin K in the body. Check with your doctor if you have any concerns.

Types of minerals and their functions

There are hundreds of minerals - they are usually classified as either major or trace
minerals.

chapters.title: Section 28
chapters.content:
Although the amount you need differs between minerals, major (or macrominerals)
are generally required in larger amounts. Some examples include calcium,
phosphorus, potassium, sulphur, sodium, chloride, magnesium.

Trace minerals (microminerals), although equally important to bodily functions are
required in smaller amounts. Examples include iron, zinc, copper, manganese, and
iodine selenium.

Some of the important minerals to keep us healthy are listed below.

Calcium

Calcium

chapters.title: Section 29
chapters.content:
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/calcium)

is vital to keep our bones strong and healthy. If you don’t get enough calcium, your
https://(www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 9/17

11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

bones will eventually become weak and brittle and can lead to conditions like

osteoporosis. Calcium helps:

¢ strengthen bones and teeth

e¢ regulate muscle and heart function

¢ blood clotting

chapters.title: Section 30
chapters.content:
e transmission of nervous system messages

* enzyme function.

Food sources of calcium

At different life stages, our calcium needs vary. It is better to get calcium from foods

than from calcium supplements.

Good sources of calcium include dairy foods like milk, yoghurt and cheese and some

plant-based foods with added calcium (for example, soymilk, tofu

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/soybeans)

and breakfast cereals).

chapters.title: Section 31
chapters.content:
Other sources of calcium include almonds, bok choy, kale, parsley, broccoli and

watercress.

lodine

lodine

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/iodine)

is essential to make thyroid hormones. These hormones control your metabolic rate

(the rate your body uses energy when it is resting). They also help your brain and

body grow and develop.

Food sources of iodine

We only need a very small amount of iodine in our diet. lodine is found naturally in

foods such as:

chapters.title: Section 32
chapters.content:
e dairy products
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Dairy-and-dairy-aglternatives)

e seafood

e seaweed (kelp)

* eggs

https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 10/17

11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

« some vegetables.

lodine can also be found in iodised salt. All bought breads (except organic
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/organic-food)

) in Australia are fortified with iodised salt.

chapters.title: Section 33
chapters.content:
You are likely to be getting enough iodine through your diet. However, if you are
deficient and need to take a supplement, be guided by your doctor. Too much iodine
can be harmful, especially if you have an underlying thyroid disorder.

Iron

lron

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/iron)

chapters.title: Section 34
chapters.content:
is an important mineral that is involved in various bodily functions, including the
transport of oxygen in the blood the provision of energy to cells. It also vital to help
our immune system function effectively to fight infection.

Food sources of iron

Iron can be found in animal and plant foods including:

e red meat and offal

e fish

e poultry

e legumes

* eggs

e breakfast cereals with added iron.

lron deficiency

chapters.title: Section 35
chapters.content:
Iron deficiency is common and can affect adults and children. Around one in 8
people do not consume enough iron to meet their needs.

Some factors such as certain foods and drinks can affect how much iron your body
absorbs. Also, some groups are more at risk of iron deficiency, such as babies and
young children, teenage girls, women with heavy periods
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/heavy-periods)

chapters.title: Section 36
chapters.content:
, vegans and vegetarians
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/vegetarian-and-vegan-eating)

and people with chronic conditions.
https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals WN7

11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

Zinc

Zinc is an important mineral involved in various bodily functions - growth and
development as well as immune function.

chapters.title: Section 37
chapters.content:
Zinc also helps to produce the active form of vitamin A and transports it around the
body.

Food sources of zinc

Zinc is highest in protein-rich foods but may also be found in some plant foods.
Dietary sources include:

¢ red meat

e shellfish

¢ poultry

e milk and cheese

e whole grains

e cereals with added zinc.

Magnesium

chapters.title: Section 38
chapters.content:
Magnesium is important due to its many functions in the body - including
maintaining bone health and using glucose for energy
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/carbohydrates-and-the-glycaemic-
index)

Magnesium also supports immune function and helps regulate blood pressure and
lung function.

Food sources of magnesium

Dietary sources include:

e nuts (such as cashews)

e legumes

e dark green vegetables

e seafood

chapters.title: Section 39
chapters.content:
https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 12/17

11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel

e whole grains

e chocolate and cocoa.

Potassium

Potassium is important for the nerves, muscles and heart to work properly. It also

helps lower blood pressure

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/blood-pressure)

Food sources of potassium

Our bodies are designed for a high-potassium diet, not a high-salt diet. Food

chapters.title: Section 40
chapters.content:
processing tends to lower the potassium levels in many foods while increasing the

sodium content.

It is much better to eat unprocessed foods - such as fruit, vegetables and lean

meats, eggs, fish and other healthy, everyday foods.

Foods high in potassium include:

e bananas and apricots

¢ mushrooms and spinach

e nuts and seeds
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Nuts-and-seeds)

Be guided by your doctor, some people with kidney disease

chapters.title: Section 41
chapters.content:
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/kidney-disease)

,or who are taking some medications, need to be careful not to get too much

potassium in their diet.

Sodium

A small amount of sodium is important for good health as it helps to maintain the

correct volume of circulating blood and tissue fluids in the body.

Most of us are consuming far more sodium than we need. In fact, many Australians

are consuming almost double the amount required.

chapters.title: Section 42
chapters.content:
Too much sodium can lead to high blood pressure (hypertension)

(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/blood-pressure-high-

hypertension)

and other health conditions.

https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 13/17

chapters.title: Section 43
chapters.content:
11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel
Food sources of sodium
Salt
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/salt)
is the main source of sodium in our diet. It is a chemical compound (electrolyte)
made up of sodium and chloride.
Many foods - wholegrains, meat and dairy products - naturally contain small
amounts of sodium, while highly processed foods usually contain large amounts.
Vitamin and mineral deficiencies and supplements
The fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K can be locked away in the liver and body fat,
and stored for a long time. The water-soluble vitamins, including B-complex and
vitamin C, are mostly only stored for a shorter period.
A vitamin deficiency takes weeks or months before it will affect your health. For
instance, it would take months of no vitamin C before you developed scurvy.
Vitamin and mineral supplements
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/vitamin-and-minerals)
may be recommended in certain circumstances to correct vitamin and mineral
deficiencies - such as folate for women who are pregnant
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/pregnancy-and-diet)
or planning a pregnancy
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Conceiving-a-baby)
. Others who may be at risk of a vitamin or mineral deficiency include:
* pregnant women and women who are breastfeeding
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/breastfeeding)
e people who smoke
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/smoking-quitting-tips)
, drink alcohol
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/alcohol)
in excess or use illegal drugs
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/healthyliving/drugs)
¢ crash dieters
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/weight-loss-common-myths)
or those on very strict diets
e the elderly (especially those who are disabled or chronically ill)
e« some vegetarians or vegans
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/vegetarian-and-vegan-eating)
https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/Vitamins-and-minerals 14/17

chapters.title: Section 44
chapters.content:
11/5/23, 7:18 PM Vitamins and minerals - Better Health Channel
* women with heavy periods
(http://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/heavy-periods)
¢ people with food allergies
